extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, rhetoric, and natural philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for clear speech, correct naming/definitions, and sound reasoning (how to form, test, and avoid errors and absurdities in argument and language). Targets learners of logic, rhetoric, and natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remembrance (Calling to mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remembrance or Calling to mind: when a man seeks what he hath lost his mind runs back from place to place and time to time to find where and when he had it; thoughts run over the same places and times to find what action or occasion made him lose it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ordered mental search (fix a determinate place/period and 'sweep' it) — examples: sweeping a room, a spaniel ranging the field, running over the alphabet. This is a method for recovering past particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence / Foresight
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence (foresight, providence, sometimes called wisdom) is the expectation of future events by recollecting like past actions and their sequels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More past experience increases prudence and makes expectations seldomer to fail; nevertheless prudence is ultimately presumption because the present differs in unobserved circumstances — true prophetic knowledge belongs only to the divine. Treat prudential inferences as fallible probabilistic judgments, not certainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs (significance and reliability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Signe is the event antecedent of the consequent, or vice versa; the oftener the antecedent–consequent pattern is observed, the less uncertain the sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect repeated observations (experience) to increase sign reliability; expertise yields more signs for guessing the future. Beware that even frequent signs are not infallible because of unobserved circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjecture of the Time Past
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference about what has happened in the past from traces or analogies with other cases (e.g., inferring a state's course to civil war from the sight of ruins).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conjectures mirror prudential inferences and are nearly as uncertain; they rest on experience but remain fallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The general use of speech is to transfer mental discourse into words for (1) registering consequences of thoughts (memory), (2) signifying thoughts to others for counsel and teaching, (3) declaring wills and purposes for mutual help, and (4) pleasing and delighting by playing with words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating speech, check which of these functions it serves and whether the language chosen effectively achieves that function (memory, instruction, cooperation, or ornament).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abuses of Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Four corresponding abuses of speech: (1) registering thoughts wrongly because of inconsistency of word-signification; (2) using words metaphorically in senses other than ordained; (3) declaring by words a will that is not truly the will; (4) using words to grieve or injure (verbal harm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ambiguous or shifting signification; mark metaphors as such; ensure declarations match actual will/intent; refrain from using speech to unjustly harm (except correction where duty requires).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names: Proper, Common, and Universals
rubrics_metrics.description: Some names are proper and singular to one thing; others are common/universal, applied to many particulars (a universal name recalls any one of many particulars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the logical role of universals in abstraction and generalization; when using universal names, ensure their scope and the shared quality that justifies the general term are clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of Definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Settling the significations of words (definitions) is essential before reasoning: geometry begins by fixing definitions, and precise definitions enable universal conclusions to be drawn from particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin arguments and inquiries by defining terms precisely. Wrong or neglected definitions multiply errors through subsequent reasoning; re-examine foundational definitions when contradictions appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-to-names (classification of what can be named)
rubrics_metrics.description: Things enter accounts under four general heads: (1) as bodies/matter (living, sensible, rational, etc.), (2) as accidents/qualities (motion, heat, length), (3) as fancies/conceptions (sight, sound), (4) as names/speeches themselves (general, particular, affirmation, interrogation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When naming or reasoning about a subject, be explicit which consideration (matter, accident, perception, or speech) you are treating to avoid category confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative names and their use
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative names (Nothing, No Man, Infinite, Indecible) are useful as notations to indicate absence or to correct reckoning, even though they are not names of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use negative terms to mark exclusions and to correct mistaken admissions in an account; they are legitimate tools in precise reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant (meaningless) words
rubrics_metrics.description: Words are insignificant sounds when new without defined meaning, or when compounded of contradictory significations (e.g., 'incorporeal body', 'round quadrangle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag newly coined terms lacking definition and eliminate or demand clarification for contradictory compound terms; treat such words as nonsense until meaning is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding as speech-induced conception
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand a speech is to have the thoughts which the words and their connexion were ordained to signify; understanding is conception caused by speech, so truth and falsehood are attributes of speech, not of things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comprehension by whether the audience forms the intended conceptions; ensure wording causes the intended conceptions rather than mere parroting of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconstant names (emotive/valuational terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names for things that affect us (virtues, vices, judgments) have inconstant signification because different persons or times apply them differently (e.g., what one calls wisdom another calls fear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using value-laden, inconstant terms as premises in logical arguments; where used, explicate the speaker's sense or convert to more precise descriptive terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason defined (reckoning of consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason is nothing but reckoning (adding and subtracting) of the consequences of general names agreed upon; operations of reasoning are analogous to arithmetic and geometry where parts sum to wholes and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat reasoning as formal manipulation of defined names/relations; ensure the operations you perform (adding, subtracting, multiplying conceptually) are legitimate for the domain in question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right method for using Reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of reason is not finding remote consequences but beginning at definitions and proceeding from elements (names) to assertions and syllogisms; every conclusion requires certainty of the premises and definitions on which it rests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating arguments, verify the foundational definitions and each intermediate step instead of accepting conclusions on the authority of books or interlocutors. Re-derive critical steps from first principles when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error versus Absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Error: deception in presuming something past or future that might not be so; Absurdity (nonsense): a false general assertion that is inconceivable — words that produce no conception (e.g., 'round quadrangle').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish empirical mistakes (errors of fact or induction) from semantic/ logical nonsense (absurdities). Address errors by improving evidence; address absurdities by clarifying definitions or rejecting meaningless expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 1 of Absurdity: Want of Method (failure to begin from Definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absurd conclusions often arise because reasoners do not begin their ratiocination from definitions; they attempt to cast account without knowing the value of their fundamental terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always begin systematic inquiry by fixing definitions; treat lack of definitions as a primary source of later absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 2 of Absurdity: Misattributing Names of Bodies and Accidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving the names of bodies to accidents, or accidents to bodies (e.g., saying 'Faith is infused' as if faith were a body that can be poured) leads to absurd assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep clear ontological distinctions: only bodies can receive corporeal actions (pouring, breathing); do not conflate categories in naming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 3 of Absurdity: Projecting External Accidents onto Our Own Bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascribing the accidents of bodies without us (colour, sound) to the external object itself rather than to our perception (e.g., saying 'the colour is in the body' vs 'in the perceiver').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between qualities as perceived (in the perceiver/sense) and objective features; be precise about the locus of the property under discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 4 of Absurdity: Confusing Bodies with Names/Speeches (reifying universals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving the names of bodies to names or speeches (e.g., treating 'a living creature' as a genus existing apart from particulars) generates category mistakes and absurdities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reifying linguistic constructs; treat universals as names for shared features among particulars, not as separate substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 5 of Absurdity: Attributing Accidents to Names and Speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving names of accidents to names and speeches (e.g., 'The Nature of a Thing is in its Definition' or 'A Man's Command is his Will') confuses linguistic or conceptual relations with real properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate the map (definitions, words) with the territory (things themselves); keep analytic distinctions between definitions and ontological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 6 of Absurdity: Use of Metaphors and Tropes in place of proper words
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhetorical figures (metaphors, tropes) used instead of proper, literal words can mislead in the search for truth; though tolerable in common speech, they are not fit for precise reckoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark and limit metaphors when engaging in logical analysis; prefer literal, well-defined language in demonstrations and argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause 7 of Absurdity: Use of words that signify nothing (school cant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of terms taken up by rote from schools that signify nothing (e.g., 'hypostatical', 'eternal-now') produces absurdity because the words lack clear sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject or explicate scholastic cant and terminological abuses; require that technical terms have clear, explicated meanings before using them in argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science: definition and acquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: Science is knowledge of consequences and dependences of one fact upon another; it is attained by industry: imposing apt names and acquiring good orderly method from elements (names) to assertions to syllogisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To develop science, fix precise names (definitions) and adopt methodical procedures to derive and demonstrate consequences; science differs from prudence in being systematic and (where valid) infallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of Science (certain versus uncertain signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs of science: certain when a pretender can teach and demonstrate truth perspicuously to another; uncertain when only some particular events answer to the pretence (as in prudence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims to knowledge by whether they admit clear demonstration and teaching (certain) versus only empirical, contingent success (uncertain). Prefer demonstrable methods where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence versus Sapience (wisdom distinctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence (prudentia) is much experience; Sapience (sapientia) is much science. Prudence is useful practical dexterity; sapience is acquired science that renders conduct more infallible in principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing practical judgment, distinguish whether it rests primarily on experience (prudence) or on systematic scientific understanding (sapience). Value both but recognize their different reliabilities and domains.
